(p-120) Surat al-Insan, also called Hal Ata, al-Amshaj, and al-Dahr.

Its purpose is to warn mankind through what the Last Day indicates: the presentation before the King, the Judge, with the disobedient punished "in the fires" and the obedient granted bliss in the gardens, after all creatures are gathered, [all of them -] humans, angels, jinn, and other living beings. There will be long standing-places, terrors, and convulsions, each of which is of the greatest importance. The most indicative of these for mankind is the contemplation of his own signs and reflection on his beginning and end. Likewise, the naming of the surah as Hal Ata, al-Dahr, and al-Amshaj is without deviation or crookedness.

(In the name of Allah), the King who created creatures so that they might know His Most Beautiful Names. (The Most Gracious), who has encompassed them with His apparent blessings, singly and in pairs. (The Most Merciful), who has singled out from among them whoever He chose for His love, with inner blessing and the highest station.

* *

Since the threat against all denial was mentioned at the end of the previous surah, and [the fact] that the return is to Allah alone, and the rejection of those who think that man will be left aimless, and the proof of resurrection and the completeness of His power over it, this surah's opening follows with a rhetorical interrogative (istifham inkari) about what, by its nature, makes it certain that man will not be left aimless. It then details what He, glory be to Him, has bestowed on man: the blessings of creation, preparation, provision, and felicity. He says: ﴿Has there come upon man a span of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ That is, in any way whatsoever. "Man" here means this species, which is preoccupied with what he is for and what he is meant for, due to the greatness of his rank in reality: self-love, admiration of his outward appearance, and forgetfulness of what comes after his burial. ﴿A span of time﴾ means a limited measure, however short, of the unlimited extended time, ﴿when he was not﴾ existing in that span in a firm existence ﴿a thing worth mentioning﴾, meaning a mention that has apparent consideration in the higher assembly and elsewhere, to the extent that he would be regarded with contempt and not looked upon. This would allow him to be left aimless, without command or prohibition, and then to go back to nothingness. The matter is not so. Rather, no time passes over him after his creation without his being a thing worth mentioning, either through fermentation (takhmir) or through the completion of his form. That is because al-dahr is the time, and time is the measure of the motion of the celestial sphere (falak), as al-Razi transmitted it in his book Al-Lawami' in the commentary on Surat Ya-Sin at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor can the night outstrip the day﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40]. He said: "The beginning of time is from the movements of the heavens, for time is the measure of the movements of the sphere." End of quotation.

Adam, peace be upon him, was completed when his creation was finished at the end of the first Friday that existed. His clay had been fermented for a period before that, during which he was between spirit and body. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Allah created Adam, peace be upon him, from dust, and he remained [in that state] for forty years; then from clay for forty years; then from dry clay (salsal) for forty years; then from black mud (hama' masnun) for forty years; then He created him after one hundred and sixty years." [Al-Baghawi said: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Then He created him after one hundred and twenty years."] So, at that point, no time passed over him without his being a thing worth mentioning, either in fermentation or in the completion of his shaping. The interrogative is therefore in its proper place and is one of denial. The word hal here does not mean qad (indeed), unless the hamza of interrogation is understood before it. The interrogation is one of denial, so that the content of the statement is negated. The meaning is that man is the purpose of the world, so Time was not created except for his sake. He is therefore the noblest of creatures. This is the strongest proof of his being resurrected for recompense. Is it then permissible, in light of this, that he be left aimless, so that the container perishes while the thing intended in itself remains, and the container, which was created only as a sheath for it, endures? What indicates this from the sayings of the early generations (al-salaf) is that a man recited this surah in the presence of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "Would that this had not been!"

(p-121) Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there come upon man a span of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ is an introduction of man through his own condition and the beginning of his matter, so that he knows that he has no way to pride himself or to believe in his own lordship, and so that the divine kindnesses, the divine care, and the honor that surround him do not deceive him into believing that he deserves and merits them. ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [An-Nahl: 53]. Since in the previous surah (al-Qiyamah) the announcement of His, exalted is He, concerning the state of those who deny resurrection through obstinacy, arrogance, and blindness to reflection and consideration was mentioned, namely ﴿Does man think that We will not gather his bones?﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 3], and His saying after: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 31], ﴿but he denied and turned away﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 32], ﴿then went to his family swaggering﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 33], that is, strutting with haughtiness, arrogance, exultation, and tyranny. And [the surah] introduces him through his condition, which, if he had reflected upon it, would not have produced what was described of him. That is His saying: ﴿Was he not a drop of ejaculated semen?﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 37], ﴿then he became a clinging clot, and He shaped and proportioned him﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 38]. This is followed by what is even more pointed in reproach and deeper in introduction, namely that he was [once -] nothing: no drop and no clot. Then Allah bestowed upon him the blessing of existence, and transferred him, exalted is He, from stage to stage. He made him a drop of despised water in a secure dwelling, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, until He brought him forth and shaped him into another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators. Whoever considers his attribute of nonexistence, then his turning through these stages, whose states are abhorrent and whose passing away and dissolution are evident (p-122), and whom Allah has aided with His success, recognizes the deprivation of one described in His saying: ﴿then went to his family swaggering﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 33]. Glory be to Allah, how great is His forbearance, His generosity, and His gentleness! [Then -] He, exalted is He, clarified what He placed in man of hearing and sight as a trial for him. Whoever is overtaken [by this] is overtaken by error and commits transgression. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

When He mentioned the absolute fact of His creating, and established that man is the essence of existence, He began to mention the manner of his creation and to indicate what follows from that: that He did not create creation except for his sake, and that it is not permissible for Him to leave him unattended. So He said, informing about the state, which is the qualifier of the sentence and the locus of the benefit, that He created him only for the Hereafter, detailing the matter of bringing him into existence through the agent, the form, the matter, and the end. He emphasized it because of their denial of it: ﴿Indeed We﴾, that is, in accordance with the greatness that is ours, ﴿created﴾, that is, decreed and shaped. He stated it explicitly and did not use a pronoun, because the second (the creation of man) is specific, while the first (the creation in general) is general, encompassing Adam, peace be upon him, and all his offspring. So He said: ﴿man﴾, that is, after the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, ﴿from a drop﴾, that is, from a matter which is a fluid, a small quantity of water, from the man and the woman. Every small quantity of water in a container is a nutfah (a drop), and it is the matter which is the cause carrying the generative power.

(p. 125) Since his creation was upon diverse natures and varying temperaments, He made him strive hard against the opposing forces that contend with him, by the command of his Lord, who does not differ. And since his actions follow his character, and his character follows his innate constitution, He said: ﴿amshaj﴾ [that is, mixtures], the plural of mashj or mashīj, like khidn and khaddayn and akhdān, and khalt and khalīt and akhlāt, from mashajtu al-shay' (I mixed the thing) when I mixed it. It is so called because it comes from the semen of the man and the semen of the woman, and each of the two has parts that differ and attributes that vary in thinness, thickness, consistency, and properties, which combine with the humours, and these are the four elements. The semen of the man is thick and white, and the semen of the woman is thin and yellow. Whichever of the two prevails, the resemblance is to it. What is of sinew and bone is from the semen of the man, and what is of blood, flesh, and hair is from the semen of the woman. Yaman said: every two colours that mix are amshaj. Qatadah said: they are the stages of creation from the drop and what follows it. Just as it resembles what prevails over it from the inner amshaj in goodness and evil. The manner of its mixing is that when the water reaches the floor of the womb, it mixes with the water of the woman, then with menstrual blood, and it thickens until it becomes like curdled milk, then it reddens, and at that point it is called 'alaqah (a clot). When that mixing becomes firm, strong, and solid, until it is prepared to be divided into organs, it is called mudghah (a lump of flesh). Then, when (p. 126) the form of the organs is poured upon it, and its garment is divided, its Bestower, Mighty and Majestic, makes it flesh at that time, and He bestows upon it the rational faculty, and at that time it is called janin (a foetus). This occurs after its parts have been divided into bones, veins, sinews, tendons, and flesh. The head is rounded, the hearing is split into its two sides, and in its front the sight, the nose, and the mouth. The remaining openings are split in the body. Then He extended the two hands and the two feet and divided their extremities with the fingers. He assembled the inner organs: the heart, the stomach, [the liver,] the spleen, the lungs, and the bladder. So glorified is He who created those things from a contemptible, base drop. From it He formed the bones with their strength and hardness, and made them the pillar and support of the body, and He determined them with various measures and shapes: some small and some large, some long and some short, some wide and some round, some hollow and some solid, some thin and some thick. He did not make them one bone, because man needs movement with his whole body and with some of his limbs. Then He placed joints between those bones, and then connected them with tendons which He caused to grow from one end of the bone and attached to the other end by ligament. Then He created at one end of the bone outward projections, and at the other end sockets matching the shape of the projections so that they might enter into them. He created the head with its roundness from fifty-five bones of different shapes and joined some of them with others. He placed six in the cranium and fourteen in the upper jaw, two for the lower jaw, and the rest in the teeth. And He made [the neck] (p. 127) as a support for the head, and assembled it from seven vertebrae, containing hollows, protrusions, and recesses so that some fit upon others. He assembled the spine from twenty-four vertebrae, and the pelvis (ʿajz) is made of three parts, and at its lower end He made the coccyx (ʿaẓm al-ʿuṣʿuṣ, or al-laffah) of three different parts. Then He connected the bones of the spine with the bones of the chest, the shoulder bones, and others, until the total of the bones of the human body reached two hundred and forty-eight bones, apart from the small bones with which the gaps of the joints are filled. And He, glorified be He, created the instruments of movement for the bones, which are the muscles, and they are five hundred and twenty-seven muscles, each of which has a specific size and a specific position. Were any of them to change in the slightest degree from that, the body's interests would be disrupted. Likewise the nerves, the veins, and the arteries. Then consider how He created the back as a foundation for the body, the belly as a container for the instruments of nourishment, and the head as a gathering place for the senses. He opened the eye, arranged its layers, perfected its shape and colour, and made it so firm that the images of the heavens are imprinted upon its surface, the size of a lentil, and He protected it with eyelids to cover and preserve it. Then He placed in the ears a bitter liquid which repels insects from them, and He surrounded them with two shells to gather sound and direct it to the ear canal, and so that one may sense the crawling of insects, and He made within them a winding to lengthen the path, so that insects do not quickly reach the body of the ear canal. Then He raised the nose upon the face and placed in it the sense of smell, for deducing from odours the state of foods and nourishments, and for inhaling pleasant scents, so that it might serve as a fan for the heart. He placed the tongue in the mouth, making it a single fleshy piece, expressing what is in the soul. He adorned the mouth with teeth, sharpening some to serve as tools for piercing, and sharpening some to be suitable for cutting, and making some broad and flat, suitable for grinding. He arranged their colours and the ranks of their rows, and balanced their heads, and ordered their arrangement until they became like strung pearls. Then He closed the mouth with the two lips, and their colour is beautiful, so that they may guard its opening. He prepared the larynx for the emergence of the voice, and He varied the shapes of the larynxes in narrowness and width, roughness and smoothness, hardness and softness, length and shortness, so that voices differ through them, so that the listener may distinguish the speakers by the distinctiveness of their voices, and recognise them even if he does not see them. He made each organ of the inner body serve a specific purpose: the stomach for digesting food, the liver for transforming it into blood, the spleen for drawing off black bile, the gall bladder for drawing off yellow bile, the kidney for drawing off the watery residue, the bladder to serve the kidney by receiving the water from it and then expelling it by its passage, and the veins to serve the liver in conveying the blood to all parts of the body. The origin of all of that was the drop, small as it is, within the womb, in three darknesses. Had the covering been lifted and the sight extended to it, one would have seen the outlining and the shaping appearing upon it (p. 129) little by little, and would not see the Shaper nor the God. So glorified is He; how great is His rank and how dazzling His proof! Wonder of wonders at one who sees a beautiful painting upon a wall, marvels at its beauty and the skill of its maker, and never ceases to exalt it, yet then looks at these wonders within himself and in others, and then neglects their Maker and Shaper. Thus His greatness does not astonish him, nor does His majesty and wisdom bewilder him.

Since man is composed of a light, pure spirit and a body which is composed of desires, appetites, blame, and base things, the spirit in its perfection and the body in its deficiency struggle, each wanting to overcome its companion. Glorified is He, Who strengthened the spirit with the Law which calls to the noble characters, forbids their opposites, and explains that most clearly through the hand of a human being whom He, glorified be He, formed upon perfection, so that he could be capable of receiving from the angels, and thus perfect the members of his species. He indicated this through a state which He established from the pronoun of greatness, and said, explaining the purpose: ﴿We test him﴾, that is, We deal with him by what We possess of greatness, through command, prohibition, and admonition, as one who tests, while We know him better than he knows himself. But We did so in order to establish proof against him according to what people understand, for the disobedient does not know that disobedience was intended of him, and likewise the obedient. So the obligation becomes in accordance with his assumption regarding what God has made him capable of, in terms of strength and power, which is suitable in general.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 2 (part 2 of 2):

When he had mentioned the end (ghayah), he followed it with the preparations that make it attainable, saying: ﴿So We made him﴾ (p-130), meaning: by the greatness We possess, as a result of that, ﴿hearing﴾, meaning one who reaches far in hearing, ﴿seeing﴾, meaning of great sight and insight (basirah), so that he is able to witness the proofs with his sight, hear the signs with his hearing, and know the arguments with his insight. Thus his obligation (taklif) and trial (ibtila') are rendered valid. He mentioned the final cause (al-'illah al-ghta'iyyah) first, because it is prior in being present to the mind [over - ] the conditioning factor that follows it and makes its occurrence valid. He mentioned hearing first because it is more beneficial in addressing (al-mukhatabat), and because audible signs are clearer than visible signs. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami' (the Lawami', a work of his): "And up to here the innate knowledge (al-khabar al-fitri) ends; from it begins the acquired testing (al-ikhtibar al-kasbi)." End of quotation.

This occurs through the breathing of the spirit (nafkh al-ruh). The spirit is a created thing that comes into being after the body has come into being, by the origination of the Capable, the Chooser, after the body has been prepared to receive it. Then He, glory be to Him, [bestowed upon the whole - ] the intellect ('aql), and made for it the hearing and the sight. Perhaps He singled out these two because they are the most beneficial of the senses, and because sight leads to insight (basirah), which encompasses all of them. He, glory be to Him, made this for him so that he could survey the forms of perceptible things and abstract universal sciences from them. By this his knowledge is perfected, and from this knowledge comes the defense of his self (nafs), which God, exalted is He, made the locus of obligation, so that his obligation might be complete.

That is because He, glory be to Him, composed him from the four elements, and made his well-being dependent on theirs and his corruption dependent on their corruption (p-131), due to their opposition. So he was compelled to have faculties by which he perceives what is harmful and so avoids it, and what is agreeable and so seeks it. Thus He, glory be to Him, arranged for him the five outward senses: He placed hearing in the ear, sight in the eye, taste in the tongue, smell in the nose, and spread touch throughout the whole body, so that by it he might ward off from all the limbs whatever harms them.

These outward senses issue from an inward faculty called the common sense (al-hiss al-mushtarak), which bears what they perceive, and it is imprinted there. That is in the front of the first ventricle of the brain. What has been imprinted here is transferred to the storehouse of imagination (khizanat al-khayal), which is at the back of this ventricle of the brain, where its form is preserved even when it is absent from the senses. There is another faculty whose function is to perceive particular meanings connected to individual perceptible things, such as the enmity or friendship of Zayd; it is called the estimative faculty (al-wahm). Its seat is the whole brain, but it is most particularly located in the middle ventricle, especially its rear part. There is yet another faculty whose function is to store what the estimative faculty has perceived of particular meanings; it is called the retentive faculty (al-hafizah) in one respect and the faculty of memory (al-dhakirah) in another, and its seat is the rear ventricle of the brain. There is another faculty whose function is to search those storehouses, to combine some of their deposits with others, and to separate some of them from others; its seat and authority are at the front of the middle ventricle. This faculty (p-132) is called the compositive faculty (al-mukhayyilah) in view of the estimative faculty's handling of it, and the reflective faculty (al-mufakkirah) in view of the self's use of it. Divine wisdom has ordained that what perceives corporeal forms be placed first, and what perceives spiritual meanings be placed last, with the faculty that manages both in between, through judgment and recall of the likenesses that have been effaced from both sides.

Then these faculties continue to serve what is above them, just as the five senses served them, until they become the acquired intellect (al-'aql al-mustafad), which is a power of the soul by which intelligibles become present to it in actuality [ in actuality, and this intellect is the ultimate goal of the human's seeking pursuit, and it is the absolute chief, served by the actual intellect ('aql bi'l-fi'l) - ] the second, and it is what is served by the material intellect (al-'aql al-haylani), likened to hyle (al-hayula), which is empty in itself of all forms. It is a faculty whose function is pure readiness to grasp intelligibles, by using the senses to survey particulars and to extrapolate from them. All of these are served by the practical intellect (al-'aql al-'amali), which is the theoretical faculty (al-quwwah al-nazariyyah), served by the estimative faculty, which is served by what comes after it, the retentive faculty, and what comes before it, the compositive and reflective faculties, both served by the imagination, which is served by the common sense, which is served by the outward senses.

[p-133] When it is as if it were said: "Suppose He created him thus; then what?" he said, as a cure for the perplexity of this question and an explanation of the blessing of provision: **﴿Indeed, We﴾**, meaning with what belongs to Us of greatness, **﴿guided him﴾**, meaning made clear to him for the sake of the trial, **﴿to the way﴾**, meaning the clear path, which in reality has no path other than it. It is the path of good, and whoever swerves from it goes astray. This was through what He sent down of the Books, what He sent of the Messengers, and what He set up of signs in the souls and on the horizons, and what He gave him of insight by which he distinguishes between the truthful and the liar, between the speech of creatures and the speech of the Creator, and between truth and falsehood, and what is similar to these.

When man, in respect of clarity, has two categories, and the context is to explain his magnification, that he is the essence of existence and the purpose of creation, he said, placing as a circumstantial clause from his pronoun in "guided him," swearing to him and placing first the oath by which He completed the blessing of guidance through clarity by creating faith, because that is more fitting to the mention of his honouring, by making him the essence of being; and by His saying, in the context of the beginning of creation, "Indeed My mercy has preceded My wrath," expressing it with the active participle free of intensification, because no one can thank for all blessings, so he is not called grateful except by a bounty [from] his Lord upon him: **﴿either grateful﴾**, meaning because of his Lord's favour upon him.

When man, because of his deficiency, is mostly never free of some kind of disbelief, He used the form of intensification as an alert to him concerning that, informing him that he is not seized except [p-134] by immersing himself in it, so that he may know the blessing of forbearance toward him, and then shame will move him to turn toward the one who is content with a little gratitude from him. It is also possible that this is understood as: whoever disbelieves in one blessing has disbelieved in all of them and thus becomes extremely ungrateful; so He said: **﴿or ungrateful﴾**, meaning extremely disbelieving through turning away, denial, worship of other than Him, and obstinacy. So His favour does not fulfil his excessive wrongdoing. He began with gratitude because it is the origin. Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition), and then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian," the hadith. Ahmad ibn Mani' narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Imam Ahmad narrated from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, and its wording is: "Every child is born upon the fitrah until his tongue speaks for him, either grateful or ungrateful." Imam Ahmad also narrated it, and Abu Ya'la, from al-Aswad ibn Sari', may Allah be pleased with him.

When He had divided them into the two categories, He mentioned the recompense of each category. He said, beginning a new sentence as an answer to one who asks about this, giving good news to the thankful one who prepared himself, by ascending through the stages of acts of worship to the realm of the higher beings, for ﴿a rest and bounty and a Garden of delight﴾; and warning (p-135) the disbeliever who prepared himself, by descending into the depths of transgressions and becoming bound to the lowest things, for ﴿an abode of boiling water and the burning of the Hellfire﴾. He placed the disobedient first, because the method of the scattered arrangement (al-nashr al-mushawwash) is more eloquent. And so that the beginning with the thankful one in the principle of the division would be balanced, so that fear and hope would be equal, and so that the thankful one would be both first and last. And because submission through threat is more complete, since it is more indicative of power, especially with regard to the people of ignorance (ahl al-jahiliyyah), among whom knowledge of the legal obligations (al-takalif al-shar'iyyah) was remote. He also frequently used, in the Great Qur'an, the call through encouragement and intimidation, because this is what the ignorant, who are the majority of people, understand, rather than proofs and demonstrations, which only the elite understand. He emphasized, to refute the disbelievers, with ﴿Indeed We﴾, meaning, on the basis of the greatness that belongs to Us, ﴿have prepared﴾, meaning, We have readied and made ready with severity and harshness, ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, meaning, those deeply immersed in disbelief in particular. He placed the easier of the punishments before the easier in ascending order, so He said: ﴿chains﴾, by which they are led and made to climb. The reading of the one who gave it tanwin (nunnation) indicates that it is very great. Likewise is the pausal reading of Abu 'Amr upon it with an alif together with the prohibition of declension (al-man' min al-sarf). ﴿And shackles﴾, meaning collars that gather their hands to their necks, in which they are humiliated. ﴿And a blaze﴾, meaning a fire, very scorching and intensely kindled.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 5:

When He had been brief about the recompense of the disbeliever, He followed it with the recompense of the grateful one and elaborated on it (p-136), as an emphasis on encouragement (targhib). For after the breaking of the threat, souls are stirred by even the least promise, so how much more by its most complete and most sublime form. Thus He said, resuming and emphasizing the denial of the disbeliever, and making clear, by mentioning wine in this description, that they are at the furthest extent of pleasant living, because drinking it entails all of its preliminaries and completions: ﴿Indeed, the righteous (al-abrar)﴾, singled out from the generality of the grateful. It is the plural of barr, like arbab as the plural of rabb, or of barr (bārr), like ashhad as the plural of shahid. They are those whose aspirations rose above base things, so that the springs of wisdom appeared in their hearts, and they spent themselves away from the closeness of this world. ﴿They drink﴾, that is, what they desire to drink, ﴿from a cup﴾, that is, of wine, as al-Hasan said. "Cup" (ka's) is the name for a vessel in which it is held. ﴿Whose mixture is﴾, that is, the thing it is mixed with, ﴿camphor﴾, that is, for its coolness, its sweetness, and the goodness of its fragrance. The mention of the verb "kāna" (was/is) indicates that it has a great role in the mixing, as though it were of the very nature of its constitution, not as is customarily known.

Since the camphor is, in the form we know it, solid, he (the Exalted) made clear that it is not so there. So He said, as a substitute for "kāfūr": ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾, i.e., mixed with it, just as you say, "I drank the water with honey." ﴿The servants of Allah﴾, i.e., the special companions of the Greatest King and His friends, drink whatever drink they wish.

Since the mixing requires effort in conveying it, He said: ﴿they make it gush forth in abundance﴾, i.e., while they split it open and channel it with the utmost abundance, directing it wherever they wish, from their dwellings, however high they are, and elsewhere.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 7:

When He had mentioned their recompense for their righteousness, which made clear their gratitude, He followed it with its detailed explanation. So He said, beginning a new sentence as an explanation: because their gratitude consisted of exalting the command of Allah, showing compassion toward the creatures of Allah, and cultivating the outer and inner self, since they combined nobility of disposition and refinement of temperament, which drives one to accept what is possible and which calls for belief in the unseen: ﴿They fulfill﴾, that is, on the basis of continuity, ﴿the vow﴾. This is a metaphor for their fulfilling all kinds of worship, because whoever fulfills what he has obligated upon himself is, with what Allah has obligated without an intermediary, all the more fulfilling. It is also possible that the vow here means everything He, glorified is He, has enjoined upon them.

When their fulfilment indicated the soundness of their natures, He said, conjoining as an indication that they combine the two conjoined matters, so they perform fulfilment not out of fear but out of nobility of disposition: ﴿and they fear﴾, that is, along with their performance of the obligations, ﴿a Day whose evil is widespread﴾, that is, a state inherent in its nature, ﴿its evil﴾, that is, what it contains of hardships, ﴿spreading far and wide﴾, that is, existing in its flying about, an existence as if it were with utmost eagerness for it, so it is at the utmost extent of dispersal. And fear is the clearest proof of the cultivation of the inner self. They said: fear has never left a heart without ruining it; whoever fears travels by night, and whoever travels by night reaches the destination. So fear is for avoiding evil, and fulfilment is for attaining good.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 8:

Since whoever fears something strives to secure safety from it by every means that might benefit him [fihi-], and since He had mentioned their taking refuge in what is obligatory (wajib), He followed it with what is recommended (mandub), as an indication that they have no inclination toward this world and no trust in it. For they combined nobility of disposition with fidelity and tenderness of heart, and the nobility of the soul in detaching itself from what perishes. So He said: ﴿And they give food﴾, meaning according to what is within their means, whether for the high or the low, constantly.

Since a person may give away what he does not himself enjoy, He said: ﴿despite their love for it﴾, meaning their love for it, a love that is at the utmost degree of their need for it and their mastery over their hearts, given its scarcity, their desire for it, and their need of it. This is as the Exalted said: ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 92], so that it is understood that they are more lavish in giving for the sake of virtue. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If one of you were to spend the equivalent of Mount Uhud in gold, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, that is, of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), nor half of it," owing to the scarcity of what was available at that time and its abundance.

After ﴿the needy﴾, meaning one in slight need, so the one in great need is more deserving. ﴿And the orphan﴾, meaning a young child with no father, whether male or female. ﴿And the captive﴾, meaning in the hands of the disbelievers, that is, more general than that, so it includes the slave, the imprisoned, and the disbeliever who is in the hands of the Muslims. It is related regarding the Battle of Badr that some of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) would give their captive preference over themselves with bread, and bread was then scarce, to the point that this captive would marvel at their noble conduct, and this was among what led him to Islam. That is because the Prophet (ﷺ), when he handed them over to them, said: "Treat them well."

Among the ruling concerning the true captive is that every person in distress is included, while they do this and their state is saying, by the tongue of the state or by speech, if he is in need of it, to remove any suspicion of obligation (mann) or expectation of recompense, emphasizing with this an indication that sincerity is a rare matter, such that hardly anyone believes it is attainable by anyone:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 9:

﴿Indeed, we feed you﴾ O needy ones, ﴿seeking only the Face of Allah﴾, that is, seeking the essence of the King who combines majesty and generosity, because He commanded us to do so. He expressed it as "the Face" because one is shy before the Face, hopes for it, and fears it when it is seen.

Since they affirmed sincerity through this, they confirmed it by negating what would alter it, and they clarified it by what cannot be except through it, saying: ﴿We do not want from you﴾, that is, for that purpose, ﴿any reward﴾, that is, any of the transient goods of this world for ourselves, ﴿nor thanks﴾ for anything, by word or deed. It seems this verbal noun (shukur) was chosen in its form like "ad-dukhul" (entering), "al-khuruj" (exiting), and "al-qu'ud" (sitting), as a hint that what is negated is what one must strive to attain. As for the like of love and supplication, these are not negated; and if they had desired any of that, it would not have been for Allah. It is narrated concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse: "that Ali, his two sons, and their mother Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with them all, gave preference to others over themselves for three days, and on the fourth morning they were trembling, so when the Prophet ﷺ saw them, it grieved him, and Jibril, upon him be peace, came to him with this surah, congratulating him with it." Enduring hunger for this period is not unlikely, for perhaps the soul may have a strong state arising from absorption in the love of Allah the Exalted or otherwise, so it descends into the body and occupies the natural faculty from dissolving the parts, so hunger does not arise, just as we observe a person remaining in an acute illness for a period without taking any food, and his body is not affected by that. Thus it is no wonder that natural functions may cease in the case of some of the travellers (salikin), and this is one of the two opinions regarding the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I spend the night with my Lord, He feeds me and gives me drink."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 10:

Since souls are naturally inclined to love reward and praise, and hardly anyone believes that someone would act without intending any of that, and since Allah, glorified and exalted is He, had bestowed His favour upon us by showing that making worship for the sake of fearing Him and hoping in Him does not detract from sincerity (al-ikhlas), they confirmed their statement with emphasis by saying: ﴿Indeed, we fear﴾. And since fear of the Benefactor, considered in terms of His kindness, necessitates fear of Him considered in terms of His might, majesty and sovereignty, a fortiori, they said: ﴿from our Lord﴾, i.e., the Creator of us [the Benefactor to us -] ﴿a Day﴾, i.e., the terrors of a Day that is - at the extreme of greatness. They explained its greatness by saying: ﴿stern﴾, i.e., constricting. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. They attributed sternness (al-'abus) to it because in its severity it is like a furious lion, so it necessitates the frowning of faces in it, or [it is -] the frowning of its people, like the hadith: "Its night is standing in prayer and its day is fasting, and a life that is pleasing." ﴿distressing﴾, i.e., long. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Or it means extremely stern, gathering evil, like one who gathers [what -] between his eyes (frowning). It is derived from al-qatr (contraction), because its day is frowning, and the mim was added to it and it was intensified by its form (sigha). It refers to the Day of Resurrection. It is said: iqmatarra al-yawm, so he is muqmatirr, when it is difficult and severe.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 11:

When their act was purely for God, He made their reward its consequence, so He said, informing that He repelled from them harms and brought them delights: ﴿So Allah protected them from the evil of that Day﴾, that is, the Greatest King, because of their fear, ﴿the evil of that day﴾, that is, the magnificent one. He alluded to the outward bliss by His saying: ﴿and gave them radiance﴾, that is, a great welcoming in it and in other than it, ﴿radiance﴾ (p-142), that is, goodness and a blessing that appears upon their faces, and a pleasant life; and to the inward bliss by His saying: ﴿and joy﴾, that is, lasting in their hearts, in contrast to their fear in this world and the frowning of the disbelievers in the Hereafter and their disgrace. This indicates that describing the Day as "frowning" serves to emphasize the intensity of the frowning of its people. He alluded to the dwelling by His saying:

He rewarded them for their patience (﴿وجَزاهم بِما صَبَرُوا﴾) — that is, because of what they had brought about of patience in worship, in keeping to obedience and avoiding disobedience, in restraining themselves from good things, and in giving up what they loved. ﴿A garden﴾ (﴿جَنَّةً﴾), that is, a comprehensive orchard from which they eat whatever they desire, as a recompense for what they used to feed others. And when he mentioned what covers the inner self, he mentioned what covers the outer self, saying: ﴿And silk﴾ (﴿وحَرِيرًا﴾), that is, it is of the utmost splendor.

When he had mentioned that He had sufficed them against the one who frightens them and had granted them Paradise, he followed it with their state therein and its state, saying, indicating their constant ease: ﴿Reclining therein﴾, that is, [because -] whatever they desired was brought to them without any need for movement at all. He indicated the royal state by his words ﴿on couches﴾, that is, the high beds that are within canopies. An *arīkah* is not called that except when a canopy (*ḥajlah*) is present. [And -] some of them said: it is a couch upholstered within a dome, on which are its *shawār* and its *najd*, that is, its furnishings. It also points to the wives, because the custom holds that couches are not without them; rather, they are for them, for the husbands to enjoy them thereon.

Since the houses and gardens of this world need to be moved from one place to another because of heat or cold, he made clear that the whole land of Paradise and its chambers are equal in the pleasure of life, the abundance of shade, and the moderation of conditions. So he said, negating the harm of heat and then cold: ﴿They see therein﴾, that is, neither with their eyes nor with their insight at all, ﴿a sun﴾, that is, nor a moon, ﴿nor﴾, that is, nor do they see therein, also with their insight, that is, they do not feel what is called ﴿zamharīr﴾, that is, severe, disturbing cold, nor heat. So the verse is of the *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which one term is omitted on each side and the other is left to indicate it): by negating the sun first, it indicates the negation of the moon, because its appearance is by the sun, since its light is acquired from the light of the sun. By negating the *zamharīr*, which is the cause of cold, second, it indicates the negation of the heat that the sun causes. Thus this conveys that Paradise is independent of the two luminaries, because it is luminous by its own essence, and its people have no need to know time, since there is no obligation of worship therein in any way; and that it is always shaded and moderate, because the cause of heat now is the sun's proximity to the point directly above the heads, and the cause of cold is its distance from that.

Since their description, as previously mentioned, is "a shade-giving and temperate Garden," he joined to it with the conjunction "and" (waw), indicating that this attribute is firmly established and that it coexists with what came before, His saying: ﴿and near to them the shade thereof﴾, meaning close to the height (of the branches), without anything arising from it that would disturb the temperateness. ﴿And its clusters are made low, easy to reach﴾: "qutuf" is the plural of "qitf" (with a kasra), which is the cluster, and it is also a term for fruits that are plucked, i.e., gathered. ﴿Made low﴾ means that their picking is easy, with a great facilitation, so that the hand is not turned away from them at all, and no obstacle stands in the way of anyone who wishes to take them, in whatever state he is, whether reclining or otherwise. If they are seated, the clusters hang down to them; if they are standing, [and -] the clusters are on the ground, they rise up to them. This is a recompense for them for having made themselves submissive to the command of God.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 15:

Since the circulating of the vessels is renewed, he expressed it with the present tense, and he also made it passive, because it is the intended matter absolutely, without specifying who circulates it. So he said: ﴿And there will be passed around﴾, i.e., by whichever attendant it may be, because of the abundance of servants, ﴿among them, vessels﴾, the plural of *inā'* (vessel), as a recompense for their going around to the needy with what benefits them.

Since the aim of this surah is to frighten the human being, who is rebuked in the surah of the Resurrection (al-Qiyamah) for disbelief, and since the human being is the lowest of the categories addressed in the ranks of address, he limited the encouragement regarding the nobility of the vessels to silver, without gold, which is mentioned in Fatir and al-Hajj, where it is expressed with "people." Perhaps this is for one category [and that for another category -], higher than it, while combining and alternation remain possible. As for the one who is higher than these two categories among those who believed, and those above them, they have above these two substances of jewels what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived (p-145). So he said: ﴿of silver﴾, i.e., its name is that, but as for the reality, where is the Pleiades from the hand of the one who reaches for it?

When he had gathered the vessels, he specified, saying: ﴿and cups﴾, the plural of *kub*, which is a cup without a handle, so that drinking from it is easy from any side, and it does not need turning around at the time of taking it. ﴿They were﴾, i.e., those cups were in a state that belongs to their very nature, ﴿crystal-clear glass﴾, i.e., they were in the description of glass in clarity, fineness, transparency, brightness and radiance. *Qawarir* is the plural of *qarurah*, which is that in which the drink or the like settles, from every thin, clear vessel. It is said that it is specific to glass.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 16:

When this was the end of a verse, and the expression "qarura" (flask, vessel) might cause one to understand, or to suspect, that it is made of glass (zujaj), and since glass has among its deficiencies the quickness of breaking owing to its excessive hardness, He said, repeating the wording of the first part of the second verse, to emphasise the attribution of the good qualities of glass and to explain its type: ﴿Flasks of silver﴾. That is, it combined the two attributes of the two dissimilar substances: the clarity of glass [and its transparency] and its lustre, and the whiteness of silver, its nobility and its softness.

The reading of those who gave tanwin to both words, turning away from what should by rights be prohibited from declension, points to its greatness, the extent of its abundance, and its elevation in excellence and nobility. The reading of Ibn Kathir, which limits tanwin to the first word, serves to alert that it is the end of a verse, and that the second word is the beginning of the next one, while conveying greatness, because the second word is a repetition of the first, due to what preceded in the benefit conveyed; so it is as though it were also tanwinned. Abu 'Amr paused on the first word with an alif, together with not giving tanwin, because that suffices as an indication that it is the end of a verse.

When a person does not like the vessel, nor what is in it of food or drink, to be either more than his need or less than it, He said: ﴿They have measured it﴾, that is, in its essence and attributes, ﴿with a measuring﴾, that is, according to the measures of need, without excess or deficiency, because whatever each of them desired was there, with no burden, no turbidity, and no shortfall.

When he mentioned the cups (al-akwab), he followed them with their purpose, saying, singling them out by conjunction with what is implied in the sense: "They are given to drink therein what their souls desire and their eyes delight in": ﴿And they will be given to drink﴾ by whomever they wish of their servants, who are too numerous to be counted, ﴿therein﴾ — that is, in Paradise, or in those cups — ﴿a cup﴾ — that is, wine in a vessel — ﴿whose mixture is﴾ of the utmost perfection ﴿ginger﴾, which is of the utmost delight. The Arabs used to enjoy drinks mixed with it for its aid to digestion and for making the taste and fragrance pleasant.

Since ginger, for us, is a plant that needs treatment before it can be consumed, he made clear that there is there a spring that does not need, in becoming ginger, to have the earth transform it by fermenting it within the earth until it becomes a plant, so that it changes from the taste of water to the taste of ginger, as a breach of customary patterns. So he said: ﴿a spring therein﴾, meaning in Paradise, whose drink is mixed there just as it is mixed with water.

Since ginger stings the throat, so that it is hard to swallow, he said: ﴿called﴾ [i.e.,] for the ease of its swallowing, the pleasantness of its taste, and the loftiness of its description, ﴿Salsabil﴾. Al-Salsabil, al-Salsal, and al-Salsal (al-salsāl) refer to a drink that is extremely smooth (al-salāsa). The letter bāʾ was added to it (zīdat fīhi al-bāʾ) to indicate emphasis on this meaning. They said: the drink of Paradise has the coolness of camphor, the taste of ginger, and the scent of musk, without any sting.

When he mentioned the one who goes round (al-mutawwaf), because he is the intended goal, he described the one who goes round (al-ta'if) on account of the visible majesty in his circuit, to depict the dominion they are in after they have been saved from destruction: ﴿And there will go round among them﴾, meaning with drink and other delights and pleasures, ﴿young boys﴾, meaning youths who are of an age below puberty, "The least of the people of Paradise is one who has a thousand servants," ﴿made eternal﴾, meaning that He who does not reject His decree has decreed that they shall remain so [forever], without any decline or departure from that state, although they are adorned with ornaments (al-khuld), which are rings, bracelets, earrings and fine garments. ﴿When you see them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92], meaning, O highest of creation (ﷺ), for you are the most perceptive of people in sight, or O observer, whoever you were and in whatever state you saw them in, ﴿you would think them﴾ because of their whiteness, the purity of their complexions, the sheen of their light, the reflection of some of their rays onto others, and their scattering through the assemblies, going and coming, ﴿scattered pearls﴾. This is a metaphor for their large number, their dispersal in service, and their nobility and beauty. Some have said that the pearls of Paradise are at the utmost in size, greatness and variety of shapes. It seems that he used the verb "you would think" to indicate that this is mere conjecture, not a firm judgement. Some exegetes have said: they are boys whom God creates to serve the believers. Others have said: they are the children of polytheists, because they died upon the natural disposition (al-fitrah). Ibn Burjan said: "I think, and God knows best, that they are those whose faith God, glorified and exalted be He, knows from the children of unbelievers; they will be servants for the people of Paradise, just as they were captives and servants for them in this world. As for the children of believers, they will join their fathers in age, dominion and joy for them." This is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about his son Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "Indeed for him there is a wet nurse who will complete his nursing in Paradise." For this indicates that his condition will continue there and that he will pass through states as in this world, and there is no evidence that he is specifically singled out for that.

When he had mentioned the master and the servants, he proceeded to mention the place, saying: ﴿And when you see﴾, that is, you extend your gaze, and he omitted its object so that it would be general and encompassing, ﴿there﴾, that is, there, in whatever place and whatever thing it may be, ﴿you see bliss﴾, that is, there is no turbidity in it in any respect whatsoever. And since bliss may exist in a middling state, he said: (p-149) ﴿and a great dominion﴾, that is, it does not occur to the mind [...] of the vastness and abundance of what exists and the greatness that it has, the least of them, and among them there is none of low station, who looks upon his dominion over a distance of a thousand years and sees its farthest extent as he sees its nearest, and whatever he wills, it comes to be.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 21:

When he mentioned the abode and its inhabitants, from masters and servants, he mentioned their clothing, making it a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to both the agent and the object: ״ʿalayhim״ (upon them), meaning that the servant and the master are, in a state in which it [the clothing] covers their bodies continuously. Nafi' and Hamza pronounced the ya' with sukun, so that it is a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa khabar) explaining the king, by way of resumption (isti'nāf, a new sentence not grammatically dependent on what precedes). ﴿Garments of sundus﴾, which is the thin silk. ﴿Green﴾: the majority [of readers] raised it as an attribute of ״garments״. Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr (on the authority of 'Asim) put it in the genitive as an attribute of ״sundus״, taking account of meaning, since it is a generic noun (ism jins). ﴿And istabraq﴾, which is the thick brocade worked with gold; or it is thick silk garments similar to dibaj, as said in al-Qamus. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and 'Asim raised it, coordinating it (nasaq, conjunction) with ״garments״, while the rest put it in the genitive, following ״sundus״.

Since the intended meaning concerns the people of splendid clothing and adornment, he informed about their adornment, and the verb was made passive to indicate that this was made easy and accessible for them. So he said: ﴿And they will be adorned﴾, meaning the adornment of the masters and servants was found ﴿with bracelets of silver﴾, although these vary according to the variation of rank. The secret of specifying this surah with silver and bracelets, combining within it the pleasure of adornment with the pleasure of the expanse of dominion, has already been mentioned. For it (the bracelet) is a metonymy (kināya) for that. As al-Malawi said, [in ancient times] when a king ruled over great and numerous regions, he wore a bracelet, and the king was called ״the one with bracelets״ because of the expanse, greatness and number of his regions. If he did not gather regions, he was not given a bracelet. So what do you think of one who is given the plural of abundance from that? And it reaches from the limbs what the white marks reach in ablution (wudu'), as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The adornment of the believer reaches as far as the ablution reaches." For this reason, Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) used to raise the water to the shoulders and to the shins.

Since it might be thought that some deficiency could enter the mixed drink mentioned above, as it is in this world, and he had said earlier ﴿they drink﴾ [al-Insan: 5] in the active voice, and then ״they will be given to drink״ in the passive voice, he said, using the active voice, to clarify the excellence of what they are given to drink in itself and in its being from the Supreme God, who is characterized by utmost beneficence, in a manner of greatness fitting His beneficence, glory be to Him, by what the attribution of the verb to Him conveys: ﴿And their Lord gave them to drink﴾. He expressed it by the attribute of beneficence to emphasize that [point], so he said: ﴿their Lord﴾, meaning the one who brought them into being, who is beneficent to them and who arranges their welfare, ﴿a pure drink﴾. That is, it is not like the drinks of this world, whether it be of wine, water or anything else. Rather it is supremely pure, and the description of it as a drink includes sweetness, pleasure and delicacy. Yet, along with that, it is an instrument of purification, reaching others, so no deceit or whisperings remain in their inner selves (p-151). They desire nothing but what pleases their Sovereign, which is founded on utmost wisdom, and which harmonizes with perfect and purified natures and chosen characters, with no crookedness in them. None of their drink turns into impurity, whether urine or anything else; rather it becomes exudation like the exudation of musk, and it gives a man the desire of a hundred men in eating and other things. So when he eats and drinks, his inner self is purified and musk exudes from him, and desire returns. Indeed, the hadith indicates that their desire never ends at all, for he said: "He finds in the last morsel of pleasure what he finds in the first." [Allah] does this for them, glory be to Him, saying to them, emphatically, to calm their hearts, lest they think that what they are in is by way of hospitality or the like, and so they should suppose that it will come to an end.

This is that which has preceded of all the reward. "It was" — that is, a established, fixed existence — "for you" through My bringing it into being before your death, "as a recompense" — that is, for your deeds, in which you were striving against your souls and their desires toward what pleases your Lord. So whenever you performed a deed, I brought into being from this what is its recompense. "And your striving was" — that is, in a state of permanence — "appreciated" (mashkūran). Since the intended meaning is acceptance, because the one who accepts and thanks is the one for whom the action is done, the verb "shukr" is cast in the passive form here: its meaning is that it is not lost, not even a particle of it, and it is repaid with much more than it, in multiplied increments.

When he mentioned that He had made the way clear to people, and they divided into one who sees and is grateful and one who is blind and disbelieving, He followed this with the recompense of the disbelievers and the grateful. He concluded it with the pure drink, which by its nature revives dead lands, just as the knowledge whose source is the Qur'an revives dead hearts. He also settled the hearts by confirming the recompense, and ended the speech with thanksgiving, as He had begun it. Since the guidance of all people was the aim, and this was something that is hard to believe, He said, mentioning what He had honoured the Prophet ﷺ with in this world before the Hereafter, and made the pure drink a recompense [for him] because of the connection between them, by way of emphasis. He stressed it a second time with what conveys exclusivity, because of their denial, and so that the souls of his followers would be at rest about the patience to which he urged them until the time of permission to fight:

﴿Indeed, We Ourselves﴾, meaning with the greatness We possess, which has no limit, and no other ⟨is involved⟩. ﴿have sent down upon you﴾, while you are the greatest of creation in receiving revelation [ascending in it], until the revealed became a character trait of yours. ﴿the Qur'an﴾, meaning the one that gathers every guidance, the one that guards from deviation, as medicine guards the healthy in the soundness of their temperament, and the one that heals whatever ailments may arise through what it guides to of knowledge and action. He increased the emphasis because of the magnitude of their denial, and so He said:

﴿a gradual revelation﴾, meaning in stages, with wisdom, as an answer to the questioner and out of kindness to the servants. He led them step by step through the duties of the religion in a manner that accords with wisdom. He left no doubt without answering it, taught them all the rulings in which there is His good pleasure, and brought them admonitions, manners and knowledge [p. 153] that filled East and West. We singled you out for this as thanks for your good conduct that preceded prophethood, and to keep you away from everything that defiles. Since it came by Our sending it down, it gathered guidance, because of Our comprehensive knowledge and power. There is no wonder, then, in its gathering the guidance of all creation, and it left no ambiguity for them in anything. This relates to His saying about the Resurrection: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16], which alludes to what is in al-Muddaththir that this is a reminder; and it corresponds to ﴿Indeed, We shall cast upon you a heavy word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5], which points to what is in Surat al-Jinn concerning [the matter of] the Qur'an. The summary is that most of the Qur'an is devoted to establishing the greatness of the Qur'an, for it is the primary aim of the Great Sign, which, once established, is followed by all the intended content of the Sharia. The establishment of its status, dispersed throughout the text, is at its most thorough in securing its affair. This is because when the Wise One cares about something, He opens the speech with it; when He sees someone denying it, He moves on to something else according to the law of wisdom, and then He keeps casting it in the midst of that, as though He were not intending it, and He keeps doing so until its matter is firmly established to the utmost degree and sinks into the soul from where one does not perceive it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 24:

Since it has been established that among people there are those who abandoned the guidance, which is the clear exposition, and so became blind to it through their turning away from it, he (Allah) made the following statement a consequence of this sending down and that misguidance, drawing attention to the diseases of the hearts and guiding to their remedy: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you by singling you out for this blessing, despite the misguidance of those whom He has judged to be misguided, and despite whatever befalls you [and obey Him] in worshipping Him by carrying out everything He has commanded you, with gentleness, until He commands you to take up the sword. Seek help in bearing the bitterness of patience by bringing to mind that the compassionate Trainer trains with whatever He wills, of bitterness and sweetness, according to His knowledge and wisdom. Patience (sabr) is restraining and controlling the self in resisting desire, so that it does not submit to any of the foul pleasures.

When He, glorified is He, commanded him to be patient, and the command to it implied the existence of those who oppose him, and those who opposed him, peace and blessings be upon him, were the category contrary to the grateful, namely the disbelievers, and what they called him to was sometimes mere sin, sometimes disbelief, and sometimes other than that, He mentioned the outcome, forbidding the first two categories, so that it would be known that what is left unmentioned carries no prohibition. He said: ﴿And do not obey from among them﴾, that is, the disbelievers who are the opposite of the grateful, ﴿a sinner﴾, that is, one who calls to sin, whether it is free of any disbelief or accompanied by it, ﴿or a disbeliever﴾, that is, one who exaggerates in disbelief and calls to it, even if he is great and mighty in this world, for the truth is greater than every great thing. (p-155) This is because they, despite their severe harm to him, peace and blessings be upon him, would offer him desirable wealth, and ownership and marriage to their most excellent women, on condition that he follow their religion and cease from what he was upon. The prohibition against an indefinite one is a prohibition against each of them, for each of them is in the same rank of being obligatory to avoid, as in ﴿Abandon the outward and the inward of sin﴾ [al-An'am: 120]. Likewise, refraining from it is not realised except by refraining from each of them. Had he joined them with "and" (wa), this would not have conveyed that, because negating two things does not entail negating each of them. The ordering of the prohibition upon the two attributes also indicates that if the disbelievers call him to something that involves neither sin nor disbelief, it is permissible for him to accept it.

When He forbade obedience to the two who cut one off from God, He commanded constant adherence to what connects one to God, which is *dhikr* (remembrance of God), without any hindrance. *Dhikr* is the remedy for whatever ailments may afflict the hearts of the pure-hearted merely from seeing a sinner or an ingrate. *Dhikr* takes precedence over every act of worship, even though the servants were ordered to it only as a means of attaining knowledge of God, may He be glorified. Since conceiving of things by their names is naturally the first stage of conception, He began with it in the order of instruction. This is because the soul loves what is low on account of its own deficiencies, so it needed a cause to draw it upward, and He prescribed acts of worship for it. The most excellent of these is worship accompanied by reflection (*fikr*), because it is the means that leads to the goal, and worship is of no benefit without it. Thus He said: ﴿And remember﴾, that is, with your tongue, ﴿the name of your Lord﴾, that is, the One who does you every kindness, ﴿in the morning﴾, at your rising from your sleep, which is the lesser death, and it reminds you that He gives life to the dead and gathers them all together; ﴿and in the evening﴾, at the ending of your day, and it reminds you of the ending of your worldly life and the folding up of this world in order to bring about the Day of Decision. Mentioning these two times also indicates the continuity of *dhikr*, and remembering His name is inseparable from remembering Him. It is also possible that this is a command to prayer, since it is the most excellent of physical acts, because it is the greatest form of *dhikr*, being *dhikr* of the tongue, the heart, and the limbs together. In it are prescribed verbal invocations and movements and stillnesses in a specific form, which are customarily performed only in the presence of kings. Its calling to mind the existence of the Creator, acknowledging His divinity and His uniqueness, is greater, and therefore it is more excellent. On this view, the verse is a command to the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer, for before the beginning of Islam He had not commanded anything other than these two, and those before us were commanded with these two. They are the most excellent of the prayers, and each of them was two *rak'ahs*. It is also possible that it is a command to the dawn prayer, [and the noon -] and the afternoon prayer, since *al-asil* (the late afternoon) encompasses their times, for it is a general term for the evening. As for the sunset prayer, the night prayer, and the voluntary night prayer, they are included in His saying:

And of the night, [prostrate to Him] for part of it, and the rest is for resting in sleep. ﴿And of the night, prostrate to Him﴾ — that is, pray to Him the two prayers of Maghrib and 'Isha', and He mentioned them with prostration to draw attention to the fact that it is the best of prayers. This is an indication that the night is the place of humility, and the placing of the adverbial phrase first is because of the greater hardship and sincerity in night prayer, and its greater excellence, because turning toward the side of the Truth in it is more complete, since the preoccupations of the senses from people's movements and voices and all other worldly circumstances are removed. Thus it is further from showing off, so humility in it and the complete pleasure of the sweetness of worship are fuller. ﴿And glorify Him﴾ [that is] by tahajjud ﴿through a long night﴾, half of it or more than it or less. Perhaps He called it glorification (tasbih) because the struggle of standing in it and the overpowering of sleep remind one of God's greatness through exalting Him above every deficiency, and because one does not give up what he loves of rest through sleep except one for whom God is in the utmost purity and for whom He is in the utmost love.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 27:

When he had concluded his command with what necessarily follows from the prohibition, he gave the reason for the prohibition with His words, belittling them by the demonstrative of nearness and emphasizing their obstinacy in disparaging everything he (ﷺ) mentions: ﴿Indeed, these﴾, that is, those who are heedless of Allah among the disbelievers and others, and so deserve abhorrence from Allah, ﴿love﴾, that is, with a love whose increase is renewed for them at every moment, ﴿the hastening [life]﴾, that is, and they take from it and make light of it for a short time, because of the desires that surround it, owing to the shortness of their vision and their fixation on sensible things, whose pursuit is the source of dullness and deficiency and the mine of diseases of the hearts that are in the breasts. [And] whoever pursues the causes of sickness becomes sick and is called ungrateful (kafūr), and whoever pursues the opposite of that is cured and is called grateful (shākir). And they dislike the Hereafter, the deferred [life],

﴿and leave behind them﴾, that is, they abandon it in a state which is [among] the worst of what would distress them if they saw it, ﴿behind them﴾, that is, before them, that is, in front of them, in the sense of encompassing them while they turn away from it, as a man turns away from what is behind him; or behind them, because it will be after them and will certainly overtake them, ﴿a Day﴾, that is, of it. And since what wearies a person and burdens him is called heavy, he said: ﴿heavy﴾, that is, extremely severe, which they cannot bear the weight of, due to the calamities it contains, because they do not prepare for it its proper preparation. So this verse is of the type of ihtibak (interlocking): he mentioned love and the hastening [life] first, indicating their opposites second, and abandonment and heaviness second, indicating their opposites first. The secret of this is that what he mentioned is more indicative of the feebleness of intellect through not reflecting upon consequences.

Since their abandonment of the Heavy Day was an abandonment in the form of denial, which is the most reprehensible kind of abandonment, and since their denial stemmed from their belief that He had no power over it, He said, indicating the resurrection by means of the initiation (of creation) a fortiori: ﴿We created them﴾, by virtue of the greatness that belongs to Us and not to anyone else, ﴿and We strengthened their frames﴾, that is, We fortified and perfected the binding of their joints, both the outward and the inward, with sinews, in a manner of firm construction, after they had been a drop of mingled fluid (nutfah amshaj) (p-159) in the utmost weakness. The root of "asr" is the rawhide strap with which saddle-girths are bound, or binding and fastening. There is no doubt that whoever is able to bring a person into being from a drop is able to restore him as he was. [For] if his body which He originated is preserved, the matter concerning it is clear; and if it has become dust, then His originating him from it is like His originating him from the drop. At most, he would be like his father Adam, peace be upon him; rather, he is more fitting, for his dust has a basis in life, since it once was alive, whereas the dust of Adam, peace be upon him, never had any basis in life at all. Restoration is easier than initiation in the customary course of created things. [And] for this reason He said, using the particle of certainty: ﴿And when We will﴾, that is, by virtue of the greatness that belongs to Us, to change whatever We wish of their attributes or their essences, ﴿We shall substitute their likes﴾, that is, after death, in form and in the severity of their bondage, ﴿a substitution﴾. Or the meaning is: We bring others like them as replacements for them and successors to them. Or the intended meaning, which is more fitting, is that "mathal" refers to the person itself: that is, We change their persons so that after strength they become weak, after tallness short, after whiteness black, and other attributes, as has been witnessed at times in cases of transformation (maskh) and otherwise. All of this indicates the completeness of Our power and the comprehensiveness of Our knowledge.

Since this was a great proof of the power to resurrect, humbling them, He said, emphasizing their denial born of obstinacy: ﴿Indeed, this﴾, i.e., the initial creative act, or the admonitions (p-160) that We have mentioned in this surah and in the whole Qur'an, ﴿is a reminder﴾, i.e., a great place of mention of the power to resurrect and a great reminder of what I did in the original creation, and a great admonition, for in browsing it there are great warnings for the heedless, and in reflecting upon it and remembering it there are abundant benefits for the seekers who travel the path, among those who have lent their hearing [and presented their selves, their souls being turned toward what their hearing receives]. Whoever turns toward it in this way knows that We have given him the instruments and proofs that, if he travels with it striving, he reaches (the goal) without straying. Therefore, on the basis of its being a reminder, He connected by the consequence His saying, in the language of openness: ﴿Whoever wills﴾, i.e., wills to strive toward reaching Allah, glorified and exalted be He, ﴿let him take﴾, i.e., take, with his effort, through struggling against his soul and overcoming his desire, ﴿a way to his Lord﴾, i.e., to the Benefactor to whom it is fitting that he love Him with his whole heart and strive to draw near to Him, ﴿a path﴾, i.e., a wide, clear, easy road through the acts of obedience that He commanded, because We have made matters clear to the utmost clarity, removed confusion, and cleared away all obstacles from their souls concerning whomever We will, and We have fixed that in their natures, so that no obstacle remains to following the path at all except Our will. And the primordial natural disposition (fitrah) is the most just witness to this.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 76, verse 30:

When He had established for them the will (mashi'ah), which is the locus of obligation (manat al-taklif) and which is acquisition (kasb), and it might have been thought, or claimed by some claimant, regarding the creation of acts, as the people of the Mu'tazilah said, (p-161) He said, negating independence from them, turning the speech toward their address, and although it is an address, it was cut off, to move them with compassion toward remembrance, in the recitation of the majority, and with the third-person form in the past tense style in the recitation of Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir: ﴿And you do not will﴾, meaning, at any time, any will of the wills, for this or other than it, by way of origination and independence, ﴿unless﴾ at the time ﴿Allah wills﴾, meaning the Supreme King, to whom belongs all command, and there is no command for anyone with Him, so that the meanings come into being in your souls according to what He wills and decrees, upon what He wishes of their effects. By this, what the Ash'ariyyah and the rest of the People of the Sunnah have said is confirmed: that the servant has a will, called acquisition (kasb), which has no effect except by the will of Allah the Exalted and His moving it by the power of the servant. And the doctrine of the Qadariyyah, who say, "We ourselves create our acts," is refuted, as is the doctrine of the Jabriyyah, who say, "We have no act at all." Al-Mulawi illustrated this by one who wants to cut a melon: [he sharpens a knife, prepares it, brings into it the causes of cutting, and removes its obstacles, then places it upon the melon]; it does not cut unless one presses upon it with the known pressure for that purpose. If he placed upon it something unfit for cutting, such as a piece of wood for example, it would not cut even if he pressed. So the servant is like the knife: God created him and prepared him with the power He gave him for the act. Whoever says, "I create, so my act is independent by itself," is like one who says, "The knife cuts merely by being placed, without pressure." Whoever says, "The agent is Allah," without any consideration of the servant at all, is like one who says, "He cuts the melon by pressing his hand, or with a smooth reed, without a knife." And whoever says, "He acted by his power, prepared for the act by Allah's creating it for him and moving it in that act," is like one who says, "The knife cut by pressure upon it." Thus, glory be to Him, He has carried out His custom among people, and had He willed otherwise, He would have done so. It is not hidden that this is the truth about which there is no doubt. Then he gave the reason for that by His encompassing their will, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, meaning the One who encompasses by knowledge and power, ﴿is ever﴾, meaning from eternity to eternity, ﴿Knowing, Wise﴾, meaning perfect in knowledge and wisdom. So He firmly prevents others from willing what He has not permitted, and whoever He knows has good in his nature, He helps him toward it, and whoever He knows has evil in him, He drives him toward it and imposes it upon him. And this is the meaning of...

﴿He admits whom He wills﴾, that is, whom He knows to be fit for happiness. He is not unjust ﴿in His mercy﴾, since by His wisdom He makes easy for him the path that leads to it, by granting him success in justice, and prepares for him a great reward.

When the people of justice were given good news with the present tense, which indicates continuity, and not with the past tense, lest a fault-finder among those steeped in misguidance say, "I am not fit, for He did not admit me," He joined to it what is for their opposites in a verbal sentence formed in the past tense, to inform that their punishment is already existent and has been finished. So He said: ﴿and the wrongdoers﴾. That is, He humiliated those deeply rooted in the description of walking not according to the pleasing ways, like one who walks in darkness. Thus He admits them into His vengeance, and He has ﴿prepared for them﴾ (p-163) [that is] a preparation that He has enforced by His greatness, so that it is never increased or decreased, ﴿a painful punishment﴾. The verse is of the ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two contrasting elements are mentioned, each one leaving the other implicit). He mentioned admission and mercy first, indicating their opposite second, and punishment second, indicating the reward first. The secret of this is that what He mentioned is more fitting for encouraging the people of justice toward it, even if their state is bad in this world, and for warning the people of wrongdoing away from it, even if their state is good in this world. Thus this latter detailed part returns to happiness and wretchedness, based on its beginning, which indicates that man is cared for to the utmost degree of care, and that he was created only for trial. He is either a disbeliever upon whom is wrath, or a grateful one regarded with the eye of approval. So glory be to Him who created us, causes us to die, and gives us life by His power, and Allah is the Guide.
